questions.prompt: Sort these jobs by where to start: a smaller, cheaper setup (possibly a subagent), or a stronger model.
questions.explain: General practice. Bulk, checkable or read-only work suits a small tier or a subagent. Planning, hard debugging and unfamiliar science suit a stronger model, because errors there are costly and hard to spot.

items.text: Classify 5,000 tissue labels, with 200 hand-labelled rows to check against
items.misconception: Volume alone does not need a strong tier when a checker catches mistakes, and re-running only failures is cheap.

items.text: Skim a large log folder and report which tasks failed
items.misconception: Reading bulk text is the job the docs give to subagents, which keeps the main context clean.

items.text: Plan a refactor of a shared QC script
items.misconception: A flawed plan misdirects every later step, so the thinking is worth more than the saving.

items.text: Work out why a statistical method fails on an unfamiliar assay
items.misconception: Unfamiliar science is a knowledge gap, which a small tier is more likely to have and which (per one article) effort alone does not fill.

questions.prompt: Match each symptom to the next step on the upgrade ladder.
questions.explain: Add a check first so you can see what helps. Raise effort when the agent stops early or skips checks. Re-run only failures when outcomes are checkable. Change model when a verified, higher-effort run still lacks the needed knowledge (the idea that effort cannot add knowledge is from one article, not confirmed in the docs).

pairs.left: The output looks plausible but you cannot tell if it is right
pairs.right: Add a way to verify it, such as a test or a count
pairs.misconception: Raising effort or the tier cannot tell you whether the answer is right; without a check you cannot see any change.

pairs.left: A checkable job mostly passes and a few items fail
pairs.right: Re-run only the failures at higher effort
pairs.misconception: Re-running everything at higher effort pays again for the work that already passed.

pairs.left: The agent stops early and skips checks, with a test in place
pairs.misconception: Switching model is the later rung; stopping early is a thoroughness symptom that effort addresses first.

pairs.left: At high effort and a good check, it still lacks the domain knowledge
pairs.right: Try the next model tier up
pairs.misconception: Per one article, more thinking cannot supply knowledge the model lacks, so another effort level is the wrong next step.

questions.prompt: An agent's rewrite of a samplesheet parser looks wrong, and you have no tests. What do you do first?
questions.explain: Without a way to verify, you cannot tell whether a stronger model or higher effort improved anything. Build the check first, then climb.

options.text: Write a check, such as a row-count comparison
Switch to the strongest model, then ask the same question again
options.misconception: Without a check you cannot see whether the new answer is better, so the extra cost buys nothing you can verify.

options.text: Set effort to the maximum level, then ask the same question again
options.misconception: Higher effort adds thoroughness and cost, and gives you no way to judge the result.

options.text: Ask the same agent to read its own code and confirm it
options.misconception: A re-read by the same model can share the original mistake, so it is not an independent check.

questions.prompt: Which line in this delegation plan will most likely go wrong?
questions.explain: Per the docs, the built-in Explore and Plan subagents skip CLAUDE.md, so rules in it do not reach them. State the rule in the task you hand them.

lines.text: Define a log-reader subagent with model: haiku and effort: medium for reading pipeline logs.
lines.why: A named model and effort are set in the definition, which the docs allow.

lines.text: Ask the built-in Explore subagent to survey the repo; it will obey the 'never edit raw/' rule from our CLAUDE.md, so the prompt need not mention it.
Ask the subagent to return exact file paths with its summary, then open two of them to spot-check.
lines.why: A summary can omit or distort, so cited paths let you check it.

questions.prompt: Put the upgrade ladder in the order one article suggests when output is not good enough.
questions.explain: This is one article's order (not confirmed in the docs as a sequence). Check first so you can see changes, then the cheaper lever, effort, then the model.
items: Add a way to verify the output
